**MEMO**

**From:** Engineering Lead
**To:** Platform & ML Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware Procurement vs. Utilisation Improvement
**Date:** June 2025

Team,

We have been circling the same question for three weeks now, and I think it is time I put my thinking down in writing so we can argue with something concrete rather than with vibes. The question is whether we should spend the remaining capital on additional GPU nodes or invest engineering time in squeezing more throughput from the cluster we already own. I want to be direct: I believe we should improve utilisation first, and I want to explain why, including where I think I might be wrong.

The cost argument is the one that gets raised first in every conversation, and it is the one I find least compelling on its own. Yes, a new node costs roughly what we would spend on two quarters of engineering salary, and yes, the depreciation schedule makes it look cheaper than it is because we are not accounting for the cooling, the rack space, the networking upgrades, and the operational overhead of managing yet another machine. But the real cost of buying hardware is not the sticker price. It is the cost of the engineering time we do not spend on the problems that actually compound. Every week we spend racking and configuring a new node is a week we are not building the scheduling layer, the model-serving abstraction, or the observability tooling that would make every future node we ever buy easier to operate. That is the opportunity cost that I think we are underweighting, and it is the reason I keep coming back to utilisation.

Now, the latency argument is the one that genuinely worries me, and I want to be honest about it. When our inference queue depth exceeds about forty requests, p99 latency starts to degrade in ways that affect the product experience, and no amount of clever batching or model quantisation fully recovers that tail. If we are consistently hitting that threshold during peak hours, then utilisation improvements alone will not save us, and we will have spent two months building a scheduler that cannot solve the fundamental problem of not having enough compute. I do not think we are there yet, but I am not certain we are not. The data I have is from the last three weeks, and it shows queue depth exceeding forty for roughly ninety minutes per day, concentrated in a narrow window. That is a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem, but I acknowledge that the distinction is less clean than I would like it to be.

Reliability is where I think the utilisation path has a hidden advantage that we have not discussed enough. A cluster that is running at sixty percent utilisation has headroom to absorb a node failure without a service-level incident. A cluster running at ninety-two percent utilisation does not. We have had two unannounced outages this quarter, both of which were caused by a single node going down while the rest of the cluster was already saturated. If we buy more hardware and immediately fill it, we have not improved reliability at all. We have simply moved the cliff edge further away while walking toward it at the same speed. Improving utilisation through better scheduling, model sharing, and request coalescing gives us the same effective capacity while preserving the headroom that keeps us from falling off that cliff.

The reversibility of these two paths is also different in a way that matters. If we spend two months on utilisation improvements and discover that we genuinely need more hardware, we have not wasted that time. The scheduling layer, the observability improvements, and the operational tooling we build along the way will make the new hardware easier to integrate and easier to operate. The work compounds. If we buy hardware now and discover that our utilisation was the real bottleneck, we have spent capital on idle machines and we have not built the operational maturity that would have prevented the problem in the first place. That path is harder to reverse.

So here is what I am proposing. We commit to a six-week utilisation sprint. We build a proper scheduler with priority queues and preemption, we implement model sharing for our smaller models, we add request coalescing for the embedding workloads, and we instrument the cluster so that we can see exactly where the bottlenecks are rather than guessing. At the end of six weeks, we look at the data. If peak queue depth is still exceeding forty for more than an hour per day, we buy the node. If it is not, we have saved the capital and we have a better platform.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here plainly. I could be wrong about the latency threshold. I could be wrong that the peak is narrow enough to solve with scheduling. I could be wrong that the operational tooling will be as reusable as I think. But I think the expected value of trying the reversible path first is higher than the expected value of the irreversible one, and I think the six-week window is short enough that if I am wrong, we will know quickly and the cost of being wrong will be manageable.

Let me know if you want to push back. I would rather argue about this now than discover in October that we should have bought the node in June.

**MEMO**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Platform Infrastructure
**Date:** June 2025
**Re:** Local AI Hardware — Expansion vs. Utilisation

---

We have been running four A100 80GB nodes for roughly fourteen months now, and the question of whether to buy more has come up in every planning cycle since month three. I want to put a recommendation on the table so we can stop re-litigating it in hallway conversations and actually commit to a direction for the next two quarters.

The short version: we should spend the next eight to ten weeks aggressively improving utilisation of what we already own before we spend a single dollar on new hardware. I want to be honest about why, and I want to be honest about where I might be wrong.

The case for buying more hardware is intuitive. Our queue times have crept up. Fine-tuning jobs that used to finish overnight now spill into the next morning. People are context-switching, waiting, and losing momentum. The temptation is to treat this as a capacity problem and solve it with capital. But I think that framing is premature, and the numbers we have do not support it.

When I pulled the utilisation data last week, our average GPU occupancy across the four nodes sat at roughly 42 percent over the trailing thirty days. That number is not a rounding error. It means we are paying for four machines and getting the effective throughput of fewer than two. The reasons are varied and, importantly, fixable. We have no job scheduler that understands GPU memory fragmentation, so a single 40GB job blocks a node that could otherwise run two 20GB jobs concurrently. We have no preemption policy, so a long-running experiment that someone forgot to kill holds resources for hours. We have no shared model registry, so people re-download and re-quantise the same base models repeatedly, burning I/O and compute on work that has already been done. None of these are hardware problems. They are operational problems, and they are the kind of problems that a small team can actually solve in a sprint or two.

The cost argument here is not just about the sticker price of new GPUs, though that is real and substantial. It is about the opportunity cost of the engineering time we would spend integrating, benchmarking, and debugging a new hardware tier. Every week we spend standing up a fifth or sixth node is a week we are not building the scheduling layer, the caching layer, or the monitoring that would make all our nodes behave better. If we buy hardware first, we will still need to do that work eventually, and we will have done it under the pressure of a larger, more complex fleet. The sequencing matters.

On latency, I will concede that this is the one dimension where new hardware could genuinely help. If we are hitting a hard ceiling on parallelism for a specific workload class, no amount of scheduling cleverness will conjure throughput that does not exist. But I do not think we are there yet. The latency complaints I have heard are mostly about queue wait times, not about inference or training speed once a job is actually running. Those are two very different problems, and only the first one is solvable with better scheduling.

Reliability is a consideration that cuts both ways. More hardware means more failure domains, more firmware to patch, more thermal management, more things that can go wrong at two in the morning when nobody wants to think about them. A smaller fleet that we understand deeply is more reliable than a larger fleet we are still learning to operate. We are a small team. Our operational bandwidth is not infinite, and I would rather we be excellent at running four nodes than mediocre at running six.

The reversibility argument is the one that gives me the most confidence in this recommendation. Improving utilisation is almost entirely reversible. If we build a scheduler and it turns out to be the wrong abstraction, we can tear it out. If we add caching and it introduces staleness bugs, we can disable it. The work is additive and low-risk. Buying hardware, by contrast, is a one-way door. Once we have a fifth node sitting in the rack, we are committed to maintaining it, cooling it, and justifying its existence in every future budget conversation. The asymmetry in reversibility is significant, and it should weigh heavily on a team our size.

Where I might be wrong: if our utilisation is genuinely near its practical ceiling and the 42 percent figure is an artifact of how we measure it, or if a specific workload we are about to take on requires a hardware capability we simply do not have, then the calculus changes. I have asked for a workload audit to run in parallel with the utilisation work so we can catch that scenario early. If the audit shows we are truly capacity-bound, we will revisit this decision in eight weeks with better data and a much clearer picture of what we actually need.

For now, let us get the house in order.

**MEMO: Hardware Procurement vs. Utilisation — Recommendation and Reasoning**

**From:** Engineering Lead, Platform Infrastructure
**To:** AI Platform Team
**Re:** Should we buy more GPUs or squeeze more from the ones we have?

---

I want to put a recommendation on the table before we spend another week debating this in standups. My position is that we should commit to a focused utilisation improvement effort over the next six weeks, and treat the hardware purchase as a decision we revisit only if specific conditions are met. I want to be transparent about why, and equally transparent about where I might be wrong.

The case for buying more hardware is intuitive. We are running at roughly 72% average GPU utilisation across our inference cluster, and our p99 latency on the summarisation pipeline has crept above 1.2 seconds during peak hours. The instinct is to add capacity, relieve pressure, and move on. I understand that instinct. But I think it papers over a problem we have not yet characterised, and it commits us to a path that is expensive to reverse.

Let me start with cost, because it is the most visible factor. A single A100 node with the networking and storage we would need runs us roughly $180,000 in capital expenditure, plus the operational overhead of racking, cooling, and integrating it into our scheduling layer. That is not a number we can casually absorb. By contrast, the utilisation work is primarily engineering time — perhaps two to three person-weeks from people who are already on the team. The cost asymmetry is stark, and it matters because capital spent on hardware that sits idle during off-peak hours is capital that cannot be redeployed to the model fine-tuning work the research team has been asking for. That is the opportunity cost I keep returning to. Every dollar locked into a GPU that is idle at 3am is a dollar not funding the next experiment.

Latency is where the argument gets more nuanced, and where I want to acknowledge genuine uncertainty. If our p99 problem is fundamentally a capacity problem — if we are simply running out of parallelism during traffic spikes — then no amount of scheduling cleverness will fix it, and we will have burned six weeks for nothing. I do not know that this is not the case. What I do know is that our current scheduler does not implement continuous batching, does not do dynamic batch sizing based on input length, and does not preempt low-priority jobs when high-priority ones arrive. These are well-understood techniques that routinely yield 20 to 40% throughput improvements on workloads like ours. Until we have measured what those techniques buy us, we cannot honestly say we are capacity-constrained. We might be scheduling-constrained, which is a different problem with a different solution.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I think we should be honest about that. More hardware means more failure domains. Every additional node is another thing that can fall out of the cluster, another thing that needs monitoring, another thing that can silently degrade and poison our latency percentiles. We have already seen this with the two nodes that have been flapping for three weeks. Adding more hardware without first stabilising what we have is like adding more cars to a highway that already has potholes. On the other hand, running at higher utilisation does reduce our headroom for failure. If we push utilisation to 85% and a node dies, we are in trouble. So the utilisation work must include a reliability component — we need to define what our acceptable headroom is and build the scheduling logic to respect it.

The reversibility argument is what tips me toward the recommendation. If we spend six weeks on utilisation and it does not work, we have lost time but not capital. We can then buy hardware with a much clearer understanding of what we actually need, and we will have built scheduling infrastructure that makes the new hardware more effective from day one. If we buy hardware now and it turns out our real problem was scheduling, we have spent $180,000 on a problem we could have solved for free, and we are now stuck with capital assets that are harder to sell or repurpose than they are to justify. The asymmetry of reversibility should guide us toward the cheaper-to-undo option first.

Here is what I am uncertain about, and I want the team to push back on it. If our traffic is growing at 15% month-over-month, six weeks of optimisation might buy us only a few weeks of runway, and we will be back in this conversation in November with less time to procure. If that growth rate holds, the hardware purchase may be inevitable regardless, and the question becomes whether we want to be ahead of the curve or behind it. I do not have a confident answer on the growth trajectory, and I think that is the single most important unknown.

My recommendation: commit to the utilisation work now, with a hard checkpoint at week four. If we have not recovered at least 15 percentage points of effective throughput by then, we escalate to procurement with the data we have gathered. I will own the scheduling work. I would like two volunteers for the batching and preemption logic. Let us reconvene on the 14th.
